pros: Extremely memory-efficient: exactly n+1 elements (vs 4n for segment tree)
Very fast in practice: simple while loops with bit operations
Easy to implement: ~10 lines of code for core operations
Can be built in O(n) with a single pass
Supports point update and prefix query in O(log n)
Range queries via prefix difference: sum(l,r) = prefix(r) - prefix(l-1)
Can be extended to 2D and 3D with reasonable overhead
Works with any invertible operation (sum, xor, multiplication with inverse)
Binary lifting enables O(log n) k-th element finding
No recursion eliminates stack overflow risk
Excellent for offline algorithms (coordinate compression, sweepline)
cons: Cannot handle non-invertible operations (min, max, gcd) for range queries
Range updates require two BITs (more complex than segment tree with lazy)
Not intuitive: LSB-based indexing is hard to visualize and debug
Point query requires O(log n) (unless original array is kept separately)
Only supports prefix-based operations, not arbitrary associative operations
Array must be 1-indexed (adjustment needed for 0-indexed languages)
Cannot resize dynamically (must rebuild on size change)
Not suitable for sparse data without coordinate compression
Range minimum/maximum queries not possible with standard BIT
Bit operations may be unfamiliar to beginners
Non-contiguous memory access pattern (jumping by LSB)
Limited to operations with inverse (sum↔subtract, xor↔xor)
